---
title: "Reproducible Plots: the Seed and the Order"
---

You can send your figures to a colleague, a reviewer or a journal. They (or you, in a year) should be able to produce **exactly the same picture** from the same data and the same data analysis recipe. Two things can quietly change a picture even when nothing else changes: **random scatter** and **row order**. This page explains both, and what to write in your data analysis recipe when you need an exact result.

## The short version

- **Every random layer has one seed, and it is the same everywhere.** A number you write on the layer in your data analysis recipe holds in the app, in the comparison panes, in the gallery and Blueprint, in the export bundle and when someone re-runs the exported recipe. If you write no number the seed is **0**. The app draws nothing per session: open the same recipe tomorrow and the scatter looks the same.
- **A number fixed by an audit step is the same everywhere too.** If you fix an arrangement with "Reshuffle", the plot, the export bundle, the record and the re-run all use that number, and the export lists it as a step of the audit trail.
- **Write the number you want in the recipe**, for example `random_state: 0`. The export writes every seed it used into the recipe of the reproducibility bundle, so nothing is left to a default there.
- Your standard export always contains `effective_run.yaml` with the seed of every random layer. It does **not** contain a copy of your data analysis recipe; see [Understanding Your Export](understanding_your_export.qmd) for what the standard export holds versus the opt-in reproducibility/reimport bundle (which does include the recipe, with the seeds written in).

## Random scatter ("jitter") and other random layers

When many points have the same value, they sit on top of each other and you cannot count them. **Jitter** moves each point a small random amount sideways so you can see them all. The amounts are random, so the exact position of every point depends on the **seed**, a starting number. These layers are random and take a seed: `geom_jitter`, `position_jitter`, `position_jitterdodge`, a geom placed with `position: jitter` or `jitterdodge`, `geom_sina`, `stat_sina`, and a bootstrapped summary (`fun_data: mean_cl_boot` in `stat_summary`, `stat_summary_bin` or a geom with `stat: summary`).

- With the **same seed**, the points are in the same place every time.
- With a **different seed**, the points move: the picture looks a little different, though the data are the same.

### The seed is a number

One arrangement is only one possibility. Sometimes another one looks clearer. So you can **try other numbers** (the Reshuffle button, below) until you find an arrangement you like, and then **write that number** in the data analysis recipe.

`random_state: null` and `random_state: random` are **refused**: the checker and the plot factory say so and tell you to write a number. (This rule is provisional; it makes sure the same recipe gives the same picture.)

### How to write it

Choose a number for each random layer; the checker accepts it on exactly these layers:

```yaml
layers:
  - name: geom_point
    params:
      position: jitter
      random_state: 0        # another number gives another arrangement
  - name: geom_sina
    params:
      random_state: 123
```

## What your export contains

Every export writes `effective_run.yaml` with a `seeds_per_plot` entry for every exported plot that has a random layer: the number that was really used to draw the exported picture. Next to it, `seed_source_per_plot` says where each number comes from (`audit`, `recipe`, `default`, or `mixed` when the layers of one plot differ). A plot can have several random layers: each layer has its own seed, a number written on one layer is never given to another, and `seeds_per_layer` lists every layer with its seed and source.

| What decides the seed | What is recorded in `seeds_per_plot` | Will opening your own recipe again repeat it? |
|---|---|---|
| An audit step fixed it (Reshuffle) | that number (`audit`), also listed as a `random_seed` step in `t3_steps.yaml` and in the report | **Yes** in the same session; write it in the recipe to keep it. |
| `random_state: 123` in the recipe | `123` (`recipe`) | **Yes**, always: the recipe fixes it. |
| nothing about the seed | `0` (`default`) | **Yes**, with the same SPARMVET version; write the number to make the recipe say it. |

The opt-in reproducibility/reimport bundle (see [Understanding Your Export](understanding_your_export.qmd)) carries the number each plot was exported with, written on its random layers in the recipe copy. A number you wrote yourself stays; a layer that said nothing now has the number that was recorded (0). The numbers the export added are listed in `seeds_added_to_recipe` (with what your recipe wrote there), in the bundle's `README.txt` and in `report.qmd`, because the recipe file itself does not show which numbers were added.

## The order of rows

The rows of your data can come out in a different order if nothing says which order they should have. This matters because the order can change **how a plot looks**: the order of the bars on an axis, the order of the colours in a legend, and which rows appear first in the Data Preview.

SPARMVET now keeps a fixed order: groups appear in the order they first show up in your data, ties keep their original order, and joined rows keep the order of your first table. The same data and the same data analysis recipe therefore give the same order every time.

But that order is *a* fixed order, not necessarily the one **you want**. If you need a particular order (for example the bars sorted by size, or samples in the order of your lab sheet), **say it in the data analysis recipe with an explicit sort**. Do not rely on the order the data happen to arrive in.

## Checklist before you export a figure

1. Does the plot use jitter or another random layer? Write a **number** as `random_state` in the recipe (not `null`, not `random`).
2. Do you need a particular order of bars, samples or rows? Add an explicit **sort**.
3. Export, then look at `seeds_per_plot` and `seed_source_per_plot` in `effective_run.yaml`: every plot should say `recipe` or `audit`; `default` means the recipe writes no number (the seed was 0).

## Reshuffling in the app

Plots that use jitter and have no number written in the recipe show a small **Reshuffle arrangement** button next to the plot. Clicking it draws a new arrangement and fixes it: the plot keeps that exact arrangement from then on, and the export uses it too (also when the audit trail is switched off in your app features) and lists it as a step of the audit trail. The button disappears once a number is fixed, whether by this button or by `random_state: <number>` in the recipe.

There is no button yet to remove a fixed number; edit the data analysis recipe to do that.

For the technical background (why the order can change, how the engine keeps it fixed, how to test it), see [Same input, same output](../foundations/reproducibility_same_input_same_output.qmd).
